subject: business-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What are the four factors of production?
options: Land, labour, capital and enterprise
Land, money, machinery and management
Capital, labour, profit and land
Enterprise, land, wages and interest
questions.explain: The four factors of production are land, labour, capital and enterprise.

questions.q: Opportunity cost is best described as:
options: The next best alternative given up when a choice is made
The total cost of running a business
The money spent on raw materials
The cost of borrowing money from a bank
questions.explain: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative foregone when a decision is made.

questions.q: A business adds value when it:
options: Increases the selling price above the cost of the bought-in materials
Buys its raw materials in large quantities
Pays its workers higher wages
Borrows money in order to expand
questions.explain: Added value is the difference between the selling price and the cost of the bought-in materials or inputs.

questions.q: A carpenter buys wood and materials for $40 and sells a finished table for $110. How much value has been added?
questions.explain: Added value = selling price ($110) minus cost of bought-in materials ($40) = $70.

questions.q: Which of the following is a typical characteristic of a successful entrepreneur?
options: A willingness to take risks
A wish to avoid all forms of risk
Relying only on others for ideas
Preferring job security to independence
questions.explain: Entrepreneurs are typically risk-takers who are innovative, hard-working and self-confident.

questions.q: Which activity belongs to the primary sector?
options: Coal mining
Car manufacturing
Banking
Retailing
questions.explain: The primary sector extracts or uses natural resources, such as mining, farming and fishing.

questions.q: The tertiary sector of the economy is concerned with:
options: Providing services
Extracting raw materials
Manufacturing goods
Growing crops
questions.explain: The tertiary sector provides services such as banking, retailing and transport.

questions.q: De-industrialisation refers to:
options: A decline in the relative importance of the secondary sector and growth of the tertiary sector
The growth of the primary sector at the expense of services
A steady increase in manufacturing output
The closure of all service businesses
questions.explain: De-industrialisation is the fall in the relative importance of manufacturing and the rise of the service sector.

questions.q: A key difference between the public sector and the private sector is that:
options: Public sector organisations are owned and controlled by the government
Private sector businesses are always run by the government
Public sector organisations always aim to maximise profit
Private sector businesses cannot sell goods or services
questions.explain: The public sector is owned and controlled by the government, whereas the private sector is owned by private individuals.

questions.q: A business fishes in the sea and sells its catch to a canning factory. In which sector does the fishing business operate?
options: Primary
Secondary
Tertiary
Public
questions.explain: Fishing extracts a natural resource, so it belongs to the primary sector.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common way of measuring the size of a business?
options: Number of employees
Number of managers' meetings
The age of the owner
The number of suppliers contacted
questions.explain: Business size is commonly measured by number of employees, capital employed, value of output or market share.

questions.q: Internal (organic) growth occurs when a business:
options: Expands by increasing its own output, for example by opening new branches
Merges with another business
Takes over a competitor
Forms a joint venture with a rival
questions.explain: Internal growth comes from a business expanding its own operations, while external growth involves mergers or takeovers.

questions.q: Horizontal integration takes place when a business joins with another business that is:
options: In the same industry and at the same stage of production
A supplier of its raw materials
In a completely different industry
One of its retail customers
questions.explain: Horizontal integration is a merger or takeover of a business in the same industry at the same stage of production.

questions.q: A bakery takes over the flour mill that supplies it with flour. This is an example of:
options: Backward vertical integration
Forward vertical integration
Horizontal integration
Conglomerate integration
questions.explain: Merging with a supplier at an earlier stage of production is backward vertical integration.

questions.q: One reason why some businesses choose to remain small is that:
options: The owner may wish to keep control and the market may be small
Small businesses always make higher profits than large ones
Small businesses are not legally allowed to grow
Growth always reduces the quality of products
questions.explain: Businesses may stay small because of the owner's objectives, limited finance or the small size of the market.

questions.q: Limited liability means that:
options: Shareholders can only lose the money they have invested in the company
Owners are personally responsible for all the debts of the business
The business can only sell a limited number of products
The company has a limited lifespan
questions.explain: Limited liability limits owners' losses to the amount they invested, protecting their personal assets.

questions.q: Which statement about a sole trader is correct?
options: The owner has unlimited liability and keeps all the profits
The owner has limited liability
Ownership is shared among many shareholders
The business must publish its accounts to the public
questions.explain: A sole trader owns the business alone and keeps all profits but has unlimited liability for its debts.

questions.q: An entrepreneur wants to raise a large amount of capital by selling shares to the general public on the stock exchange. Which form of organisation is most suitable?
options: Public limited company (plc)
Sole trader
Partnership
Private limited company (Ltd)
questions.explain: Only a public limited company can sell its shares to the general public on the stock exchange.

questions.q: A stakeholder in a business is:
options: Any individual or group with an interest in the business
Only the owner of the business
Only the customers of the business
A person who owns shares in every company
questions.explain: A stakeholder is any person or group with an interest in, or affected by, the activities of a business.

questions.q: The objectives of different stakeholders can conflict because:
options: Workers may want higher wages while owners want higher profits
All stakeholders always share exactly the same aims
Customers and suppliers never disagree
The government has no interest in businesses
questions.explain: Stakeholder objectives often conflict; for example, higher wages for workers reduce the profit available to owners.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Business Studies (0450) syllabus; Understanding Business Activity
